AI.motivation: To develop a robust and experimentally feasible force sensing scheme that achieves quantum-enhanced sensitivity scaling without requiring entanglement or other non-classical resources, addressing the practical challenges of implementing quantum-enhanced protocols.
AI.method: Utilizes coherent averaging across a chain of N optomechanical cavities unidirectionally coupled via a laser beam; the beam accumulates phase shifts induced by a common external force acting on mechanical elements as it propagates through the cavity chain.
AI.result: Achieves Heisenberg-limited sensitivity scaling (1/N) typically associated with quantum-enhanced protocols using a fully classical approach, providing robust and experimentally feasible precision sensing.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates that quantum-enhanced sensitivity scaling can be achieved through classical coherent averaging, opening a new pathway for leveraging coherent light-matter interactions for force sensing applications ranging from gravitational field measurements to dark matter detection.

title: Hybrid Method of Efficient Simulation of Physics Applications for a Quantum Computer
summary: Quantum chemistry and materials science are among the most promising areas for demonstrating algorithmic quantum advantage and quantum utility due to their inherent quantum mechanical nature. Still, large-scale simulations of quantum circuits are essential for determining the problem size at which quantum solutions outperform classical methods. In this work, we present a novel hybrid simulation approach, forming a hybrid of a fullstate and a Clifford simulator, specifically designed to address the computational challenges associated with the time evolution of quantum chemistry Hamiltonians. Our method focuses on the efficient emulation of multi-qubit rotations, a critical component of Trotterized Hamiltonian evolution. By optimizing the representation and execution of multi-qubit operations leveraging the Pauli frame, our approach significantly reduces the computational cost of simulating quantum circuits, enabling more efficient simulations. Beyond its impact on chemistry applications, our emulation strategy has broad implications for any computational workload that relies heavily on multi-qubit rotations. By increasing the efficiency of quantum simulations, our method facilitates more accurate and cost-effective studies of complex quantum systems. We quantify the performance improvements and computational savings for this emulation strategy, and we obtain a speedup of a factor $\approx 18$ ($\approx 22$ with MPI) for our evaluated chemistry Hamiltonians with 24 qubits. Thus, we evaluate our integration of this emulation strategy into the Intel Quantum SDK, further bridging the gap between theoretical algorithm development and practical quantum software implementations.

AI.tldr: A hybrid quantum simulation method combining full-state and Clifford simulators achieves ~18-22× speedup for quantum chemistry Hamiltonians by optimizing multi-qubit rotation emulation using Pauli frame techniques.
AI.motivation: Quantum chemistry and materials science are promising for demonstrating quantum advantage, but large-scale quantum circuit simulations are needed to determine when quantum solutions outperform classical methods. Current simulation approaches face computational challenges with time evolution of quantum chemistry Hamiltonians.
AI.method: A novel hybrid simulation approach combining full-state and Clifford simulators, specifically designed for quantum chemistry Hamiltonian time evolution. The method focuses on efficient emulation of multi-qubit rotations (critical for Trotterized Hamiltonian evolution) by optimizing representation and execution using the Pauli frame.
AI.result: The approach significantly reduces computational cost of simulating quantum circuits, achieving speedup factors of approximately 18× (22× with MPI) for evaluated chemistry Hamiltonians with 24 qubits. The method enables more efficient simulations and facilitates more accurate, cost-effective studies of complex quantum systems.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid simulation method provides substantial performance improvements for quantum chemistry simulations and has broad implications for any computational workload relying heavily on multi-qubit rotations. Integration into the Intel Quantum SDK bridges the gap between theoretical algorithm development and practical quantum software implementations.

title: Limitations of SVD-Based Diagnostics for Non-Hermitian Many-Body Localization with Time-Reversal Symmetry
summary: Singular value decomposition (SVD) has been used to construct Hermitian-like diagnostics for non-Hermitian many-body systems, but its reliability for identifying many-body localization (MBL) transitions -- particularly in time-reversal-symmetry (TRS) preserving settings -- remains unclear. Here we benchmark SVD-based diagnostics against exact diagonalization (ED) in TRS-preserving non-Hermitian hard-core-boson chains with nonreciprocal hopping, considering three representative potentials: a quasiperiodic potential, random disorder, and a Stark potential. We compare spectral statistics, half-chain entanglement entropy, inverse participation ratio, and spectral form factors. For the quasiperiodic and random-disorder models, ED yields mutually consistent transition estimates, whereas SVD systematically shifts the inferred critical disorder strength to larger values and can lead to different phase assignments. In contrast, for the clean Stark model ED and SVD locate a consistent critical tilt. Our results show that while SVD-based diagnostics capture qualitative trends, they are not generically reliable for quantitatively locating the MBL transition in TRS-preserving non-Hermitian many-body systems.
